root.note: From barr ‘open country’, as opposed to the city.

history: A barrio was once the part of town that didn't quite count. Arabic barr meant open country as opposed to the city, and barrī, ‘of the country’, was used for what was built outside the walls. In Andalusian Arabic it meant the outer, less urban parts of a town. Spanish kept both senses of the Arabic word at first: a settlement right against the walls, and one further out. Today the meaning has moved on, and your barrio can be in the very centre of Madrid. When you look for a flat, the barrio is often the first thing people ask about. Portuguese bairro and Catalan barri are the same word.
historyEinfach: Barrio means ‘neighbourhood’. It is an Arabic word. The Arabic word meant ‘outside’, in the country, not in the city. So a barrio was outside the city walls. Later, cities grew. Now a barrio can be in the centre of the city. Portuguese bairro and Catalan barri are the same word.

elsewhere.text: In Arabic the word kept the sense of wild, open land, while Spanish moved it into town.
Portuguese bairro has the same history and the same meaning.
